docs.title: @coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance
docs.text:
Behavioral safety contracts document positive and negative inputs, parameter boundaries, state isolation, and cases that require manual migration.

Rule suites require nonempty valid and invalid fixtures, named should cases, explicit diagnostics, and concrete autofix outputs. All 83 rules also run against shared TypeScript, JSX, optional-access, and Jest-chain parsing fixtures. See the contributor guide for validation requirements.

83 opinionated ESLint rules for TypeScript teams that refuse to compromise on code quality.

Supports ESLint 8.57+, 9.x, and 10.x

docs.title: Why Zero Tolerance?
docs.text:
Most linting setups start strict and erode over time. A scattered eslint-disable here, an any cast there, and before long the rules exist in name only.

This plugin takes the opposite approach. Every rule earns its place, every violation is actionable, and the codebase stays honest.

docs.title: What It Covers
docs.text:
@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance provides rules across eight categories:

Category What it enforces Type Safety Ban unsafe assertions (as, !), unsafe JSON parsing, literal unions, inline imports, and untyped exports Code Quality Limit function size and parameters, eliminate placeholders, magic values, immutability, and sort order Testing Require should-prefixed descriptions, await async assertions, and prevent skipped assertions and leaky mocks Bug Prevention Flag identical expressions, redundant booleans, missing awaits, floating promises, missing IO timeouts, and flag arguments Error Handling Require new Error() throws, ban empty catches, encourage Result-style returns Imports Keep barrels clean, ban risky imports, block injection sinks, and prevent upward traversal Documentation Require JSDoc on functions, enforce BDD specs, mandate optional chaining and readonly props Naming Enforce I-prefixed interfaces

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
npm install --save-dev @coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance

// eslint.config.js (ESLint 9+ Flat Config)
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default [zeroTolerance.configs.recommended];

See the Getting Started guide for full setup instructions and the Rules reference for descriptions of every rule.

docs.text:
Use the rule reference to choose checks and review examples, options, and limits. Enable require-error-cause individually to preserve original exceptions.

For promise handling, unsafe types, callback returns, and branching limits, see additional code-quality checks.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: @coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance ships with four built-in config presets so you can go from zero to linting in one line.

docs.title: Preset Overview
docs.text: Preset Severity Use case recommended warn Gradual adoption; shows violations without breaking the build strict error New projects or full zero-tolerance enforcement; fails on any violation legacy-recommended warn ESLint 8 .eslintrc format legacy-strict error ESLint 8 .eslintrc format

docs.title: Preset Enum
docs.text:
Internally, flat-config preset selection is typed with a Preset enum:

  • Preset.Recommended = 'recommended'
  • Preset.Strict = 'strict'

This enum is used by the shared config/rule builders to avoid stringly-typed preset branching.

docs.title: recommended
docs.text:
Most rules enabled at warn (with a few documented exceptions disabled). Function body limit: 30 lines. Parameter limit: 4.

eslint.config.js
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default [zeroTolerance.configs.recommended];

docs.title: strict
docs.text:
All rules enabled at error. Function body limit: 25 lines. Parameter limit: 4.

eslint.config.js
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default [zeroTolerance.configs.strict];

docs.title: Disabling Individual Rules
docs.text:
Override any rule to off inside your config:

eslint.config.js
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default [
  zeroTolerance.configs.recommended,
  {
    rules: {
      // Disable rules that don't suit your project
      'zero-tolerance/sort-functions': 'off',
    },
  },
];

docs.title: Configuring Rule Options
docs.text: Multiple rules accept an options object:

docs.title: max-function-lines
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/max-function-lines': ['warn', { max: 50 }]

docs.title: max-params
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/max-params': ['error', { max: 3 }]

docs.title: no-magic-strings
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-magic-strings': [
  'error',
  { checkComparisons: true, checkSwitchCases: true, ignoreValues: ['production'] },
]

docs.title: require-test-description-style
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/require-test-description-style': ['error', { prefix: 'should', ignoreSkip: true }]

docs.title: no-restricted-imports-in-tests
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-restricted-imports-in-tests': [
  'error',
  { modules: ['fs', 'node:fs/*', 'child_process', 'axios', '@company/database'] },
]

Configured module names are trimmed, lowercased, normalized by removing node:, and matched by module root. For example, fs matches fs, fs/promises, node:fs, and node:fs/promises.

docs.title: no-throw-literal
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-throw-literal': [
  'error',
  {
    allowThrowingCallExpressions: false,
    allowThrowingMemberExpressions: false,
    allowThrowingAwaitExpressions: false,
  },
]

docs.title: no-parent-internal-access
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-parent-internal-access': [
  'error',
  { protectedDirectories: ['src', 'app', 'internal'] },
]

The rule matches only the first concrete directory reached after .. traversal, so ../src/foo is reported but ../shared/src/foo is not unless shared is also protected. Configured directory names are trimmed and deduplicated, and empty entries are ignored.

docs.title: Additional code-quality checks (individual opt-in)
docs.text:
Enable the checks you need in your ESLint configuration. The example below combines this plugin with ESLint and TypeScript-ESLint rules. Install @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin and @typescript-eslint/parser first. Type-aware checks need a TypeScript project; projectService reads the project that includes each file.

import tsPlugin from '@typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin';
import tsParser from '@typescript-eslint/parser';
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default [
  {
    files: ['**/*.ts', '**/*.tsx'],
    languageOptions: {
      parser: tsParser,
      parserOptions: { projectService: true },
    },
    plugins: {
      '@typescript-eslint': tsPlugin,
      'zero-tolerance': zeroTolerance,
    },
    rules: {
      '@typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises': 'error',
      '@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment': 'error',
      '@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-argument': 'error',
      '@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-return': 'error',
      '@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-call': 'error',
      '@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-member-access': 'error',
      'array-callback-return': 'error',
      complexity: ['warn', { max: 10 }],
      'max-depth': ['warn', 3],
      'require-atomic-updates': 'error',
      'no-unsafe-finally': 'error',
      'zero-tolerance/require-error-cause': 'error',
    },
  },
];
  • no-misused-promises complements floating-promise checks by detecting async callbacks where synchronous behavior is expected and promises used as conditions.
  • The unsafe type rules catch inferred or dependency-provided any values that no-explicit-any cannot prevent.
  • array-callback-return catches missing callback returns; complexity and max-depth assess branching independently of physical line counts. Adjust thresholds to your project.
  • require-atomic-updates checks stale read/write operations across asynchronous suspension; no-unsafe-finally catches cleanup control flow that overrides a pending return or throw.

See the rule pages for sequential-await exceptions, function-length options, and error cause preservation. Each rule page defines its supported patterns and limits. A passing lint check does not prove that a program is free of side effects, timeout failures, or data races.

docs.title: Recommended preset
docs.text:
The recommended preset enables all rules at warn severity, making it easy to adopt incrementally.

Start here

The recommended preset is the best starting point for existing projects. Warnings surface issues without breaking your build, giving your team time to address violations at a sustainable pace.

eslint.config.js
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default [
  zeroTolerance.configs.recommended,
  // your other configs...
];

docs.title: Strict preset
docs.text:
The strict preset raises most rules to error severity and applies tighter limits (e.g. max function body: 25 lines); see the preset table for exact rule severities.

Best for greenfield projects

The strict preset treats every violation as a build-breaking error. It is ideal for new projects or teams ready for full enforcement.

eslint.config.js
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default [zeroTolerance.configs.strict];

docs.title: Custom configuration
docs.text:
Pick individual rules and set severities yourself:

eslint.config.js
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default [
  {
    plugins: {
      'zero-tolerance': zeroTolerance,
    },
    rules: {
      'zero-tolerance/require-interface-prefix': 'error',
      'zero-tolerance/no-throw-literal': 'error',
      'zero-tolerance/max-function-lines': ['warn', { max: 40 }],
      'zero-tolerance/max-params': ['warn', { max: 5 }],
      // ... add any rules you need
    },
  },
];

docs.title: ESLint 8.x (Legacy .eslintrc)
Typical TypeScript Project Setup
docs.text:
A complete eslint.config.js for a TypeScript project:

eslint.config.js
import js from '@eslint/js';
import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';
import zeroTolerance from '@coderrob/eslint-plugin-zero-tolerance';

export default tseslint.config(
  js.configs.recommended,
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  zeroTolerance.configs.recommended,
  {
    files: ['src/**/*.ts'],
    rules: {
      // Override individual rules as needed
      'zero-tolerance/max-function-lines': ['warn', { max: 50 }],
    },
  },
  {
    // Relax rules in test files
    files: ['**/*.test.ts', '**/*.spec.ts'],
    rules: {
      'zero-tolerance/require-jsdoc-functions': 'off',
      'zero-tolerance/no-type-assertion': 'off',
    },
  },
);

docs.title: Configuring tsconfig.json
docs.text:
No TypeScript-specific configuration is required by this plugin. All rules operate purely on the AST without requiring type information.

No type-aware linting required

Unlike some TypeScript-ESLint rules, zero-tolerance rules do not need parserOptions.project or projectService. This keeps lint times fast regardless of project size.

tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "target": "ES2020",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler"
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

docs.title: Rule fix safety gap analysis
docs.text:
The fixtures for the rules below cover both a pattern the rule should handle and a valid input whose behavior a rewrite could change. The negative cases assert that ESLint leaves the source unchanged.

Rule Positive fixture Negative fixture Safety decision no-for-in Reports ordinary for..in; allows for..of Inherited enumerable key is visited by for..in but omitted by Object.keys Report without autofix no-redundant-boolean Simplifies syntactically boolean comparisons and ternaries Numeric operands, arithmetic precedence, and comments can change or disappear Preserve boolean results and parenthesize fixes; skip commented expressions prefer-nullish-coalescing Fixes a nullish guard around a locally bound identifier Getters, unbound identifiers, logical or conditional fallbacks, and comments Skip unstable reads and comments; parenthesize fallback expressions prefer-object-spread Reports empty-target Object.assign; allows explicit spread An inline getter or __proto__ source can change copy behavior Opt-in, report without autofix prefer-structured-clone Reports direct JSON cloning; allows ordinary parsing JSON drops undefined properties and serializes Date values Opt-in, report without autofix require-optional-chaining Reports repeated guards; allows existing optional chains text && text.length and text?.length differ for an empty string Opt-in, report without autofix

The opt-in rules remain available for manual review. The negative fixtures are assertions about diagnostics or autofix output, and the rule pages describe the runtime differences behind them.

Rule Positive contract Negative or state contract Safety decision no-literal-unions Reports literal unions Existing string assignments and callers must still compile Report without autofix; migrate uses manually sort-imports Sorts explicit type imports Named and default imports may initialize shared state Preserve runtime dependency order prefer-string-raw Fixes eligible literals using native String Shadowed parameters and later bindings must retain literal values Resolve scope for each literal no-floating-promises Reports local async and typed promise results Shadowed functions, async generators, missing handlers, and later chain rejections Resolve lexical bindings and terminal callbacks prefer-shortcut-return Simplifies opposite boolean returns Comments in branches or between statements must survive Skip commented replacement spans

docs.title: Choose checks
docs.text:
Each rule page explains what is reported, how to configure the check, and where its analysis stops. Enable require-error-cause individually to preserve original exceptions.

For promise handling, unsafe types, callback returns, and branching limits, see additional code-quality checks.

docs.title: max-function-lines
docs.text:
Keep function bodies short enough to read and review.

Type: suggestion. No automatic fix.

docs.title: What it counts
docs.text: Counts the source lines occupied by a function body, including braces. Expression-bodied arrows are included. The rule's default limit is 30 lines; an existing configuration can set a different limit.

docs.title: Options
Examples
docs.text:
// Three body lines, including braces.
function getValue() {
  return 1;
}

// Five expression-body lines.
const getValues = () => [1, 2, 3];

docs.title: Counting details
docs.text:
Code beside a comment still counts. Comment-like text inside strings or template literals is code. Multiple comments on one line, Windows line endings, and TypeScript assertions do not change these rules.

Line count measures size, not branching. Use complexity and max-depth separately when you also want to limit decision paths and nesting.

docs.title: max-params
docs.text: Enforce a maximum number of function parameters.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn (max: 4) Strict error (max: 4)

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Functions with many parameters are hard to call correctly, difficult to read, and a sign that the function is doing too much or that related parameters should be grouped into a structured options object. Limiting the parameter count encourages better API design.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
/**
 * Creates a new user record.
 */
function createUser(options: ICreateUserOptions): Promise<IUser> {
  return db.users.create(options);
}

/**
 * Sends an email notification.
 */
function sendEmail(to: string, subject: string, body: string): Promise<void> {
  return mailer.send({ to, subject, body });
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
function createUser(
  name: string,
  email: string,
  password: string,
  role: string,
  createdAt: Date,
): Promise<IUser> {
  // Too many positional parameters
}

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description max number 4 Maximum number of allowed parameters 
// Default (max 4)
'zero-tolerance/max-params': 'warn'

// Custom limit
'zero-tolerance/max-params': ['error', { max: 3 }]

docs.title: Parsing and fix safety
docs.text: A max of 0 is supported: parameterless functions pass and any function with a parameter is reported.

docs.title: no-array-mutation
docs.text:
Prevent changes to known arrays and tuples through mutating methods.

Type: suggestion. No automatic fix. No options.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Reports calls to push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill, and copyWithin on known arrays. Optional calls and static computed names, such as items['push'](), are also checked.

With TypeScript type information, the rule recognizes arrays, tuples, constrained generics, unions, intersections, and inherited array types. Enable parserOptions.projectService to check typed parameters and imported values.

Without type information, the rule checks array literals and local aliases whose values are not reassigned. TypeScript assertions around an array literal preserve detection. A cast alone does not prove that an unknown value is an array.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
const items = [1, 2];
items.push(3); // Reported: changes the original array.
const next = [...items, 3]; // Allowed: creates a new array.
router.push('/home'); // Allowed when the receiver is not a known array.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: This rule checks method calls, not every way to change an array. Unknown receivers are skipped without type information. There is no automatic rewrite because copying an array can change return values and how other references observe it.

docs.title: no-await-in-loop
docs.text:
Review repeated waits inside loops and allow intentional sequential work.

Type: problem. No automatic fix.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Reports explicit await expressions inside loops. An await in a nested function is checked in that function's own scope. Type assertions and optional calls do not change this behavior.

Retries, pagination, and rate limits may require sequential work. Run independent work concurrently only when ordering, resources, and error handling permit it. Limit concurrency for large collections.

docs.title: Options
Examples
docs.text:
async function loadAll(items) {
  for (const item of items) {
    await load(item); // Reported with default options.
  }
}

async function retry() {
  while (pending) {
    await attempt(); // Allowed when 'retry' is configured above.
  }
}

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Exceptions stop at nested function boundaries. A callback does not inherit an outer function's exception. A named exception allows all awaits within that function, so keep exception functions focused. Class and object method names are not matched by allowedFunctionNames.

The rule checks explicit await expressions, not the implicit waits performed by async iteration. It does not automatically replace loops with Promise.all.

docs.title: no-barrel-parent-imports
docs.text: Disallow parent-directory traversal inside barrel files.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Barrel files (index.*) should aggregate exports from their own directory. Parent-directory imports (.. and ../*) inside those files create upward coupling, blur package boundaries, and make the barrel harder to reason about.

This rule is enabled by default in plugin presets: warn in recommended and error in strict.

This rule applies only when the current file is a barrel file (index.*). In those files, it checks:

  • import ... from '...'
  • import('...')
  • require('...')
  • TypeScript import x = require('...')

Re-export declarations such as export { foo } from '../foo' are covered separately by require-barrel-relative-exports.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The rule applies only to single-extension barrel files such as index.ts, index.js, and index.mts.
  • Double-extension files such as index.d.ts, index.test.ts, and index.spec.js are ignored.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// feature.ts
import React from 'react';
import { parseUser } from '../parse-user';
const helpers = await import('../helpers');
const feature = require('../feature');
import legacyFeature = require('../legacy-feature');

// index.ts
export { parseUser } from './parse-user';
export { helpers } from './helpers';

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect

// index.ts

const helpers = await import('../helpers');
const feature = require('../../feature');
import legacyFeature = require('..');

docs.title: no-boolean-return-trap
docs.text: Disallow ambiguous boolean-return APIs outside predicate naming.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Boolean returns can be ambiguous at call sites. Public APIs should either use predicate naming (is*, has*, can*, should*) or return richer result types.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
function isReady(user: User): boolean {
  return user.status === 'ready';
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:

  return user.status === 'ready';

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/no-boolean-return-trap': 'error'

docs.title: no-chai-imprecise-spy-assertions
docs.text: Require explicit counts and invocation arguments in Chai-style spy assertions.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Sinon–Chai's .called property asserts at least one call. .calledWith(...), .calledWithExactly(...), and .calledWithMatch(...) can pass because any invocation matches. Vitest's Chai-style .lastCalledWith(...) relies on an implicit last invocation. Use an exact count and, when arguments matter, inspect the intended call.

The rule recognizes expect imported from chai or vitest, including aliases, chai.expect(...) from default or namespace imports, and Vitest expect.soft(...). It follows Chai language chains such as .to.be, .that.has.been, and computed properties. The negated .not.called property is allowed because it asserts zero calls. Exact one-call assertions such as .calledOnceWithExactly(...) and argument assertions on spy.getCall(index) are allowed.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
import { expect } from 'chai';

expect(spy).to.have.callCount(2);
expect(spy.getCall(0).args).to.deep.equal(['first']);
expect(spy.getCall(0)).to.have.been.calledWithExactly('first');
expect(spy).to.not.have.been.called;

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
import { expect } from 'chai';

expect(spy).to.have.been.called;
expect(spy).to.be.called;
expect(spy).to.have.been.calledWith('first');

import { expect as vitestExpect } from 'vitest';
vitestExpect(spy).to.have.been.lastCalledWith('last');

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-chai-imprecise-spy-assertions': 'error'

Mocha does not supply its own assertion API; this rule applies to Mocha tests that use Chai and Sinon–Chai. It does not infer Sinon spies from arbitrary object properties or inspect should-style assertions.

docs.title: no-conditional-test-assertion
docs.text: Require assertions in test files to execute on every applicable path.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
An assertion inside an if, ternary branch, short-circuit right operand, catch, switch case, or loop body can be skipped. A test can then pass without checking the intended behavior. Split the cases into separate tests or place an assertion after conditional setup.

The rule recognizes Jest and Vitest expect, Chai expect and assert, Sinon assert, and imported Node assert (including direct calls). It supports aliases, Vitest local test-context expect, supported namespace access, and computed properties. It checks test files and recognizes assertions inside promise catch callbacks. A conditional expression used to prepare an assertion's input is allowed. Assertions directly inside do...while bodies or for...of loops over array literals with a fixed element are allowed because the body executes at least once. Conditional branches inside those bodies and skippable outer loops remain checked.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
test('should select the expected value', () => {
  const actual = condition ? first : second;
  expect(actual).toBe(expected);
});

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
test('should select the expected value', () => {
  if (condition) {
    expect(actual).toBe(expected);
  }
});

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-conditional-test-assertion': 'error'

This rule checks whether a present assertion can be skipped. It does not require every test to contain an assertion.

docs.title: no-date-now
docs.text: Disallow Date.now() and new Date() without arguments.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Direct time reads create non-deterministic code that is harder to test. Injecting a clock or passing timestamps improves testability and reproducibility.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text: const timestamp = clock.now();

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
const timestamp = Date.now();
const createdAt = new Date();

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/no-date-now': 'error'

docs.title: no-destructured-parameter-type-literal
docs.text: Disallow inline object type literals on destructured parameters.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Destructured parameters already hide the original object shape at the call site. Adding an inline object type literal to the same parameter makes the contract harder to reuse, harder to scan, and harder to name in documentation. Requiring a named type keeps the contract explicit and reusable.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
interface IUiActions {
  readonly set: UiStateSetter;
}

function update({ set }: IUiActions): void {
  set('ready');
}

type UiActions = Readonly<{ readonly set: UiStateSetter }>;

const updateLater = ({ set }: UiActions): void => {
  set('later');
};

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
function update({ set }: Readonly<{ set: UiStateSetter }>): void {
  set('ready');
}

const updateLater = ({ set }: { readonly set: UiStateSetter }): void => {
  set('later');
};

'zero-tolerance/no-destructured-parameter-type-literal': 'error'

docs.title: no-dynamic-import
docs.text: Ban dynamic import() and require() calls outside of test files.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Dynamic imports and require() calls load modules at runtime rather than at bundle time. This hides dependencies from static analysis tools, prevents tree-shaking, complicates code-splitting strategies, and can introduce subtle load-order bugs. Static import declarations at the top of a file are always preferable in application code.

The rule is automatically skipped in test files (*.test.*, *.spec.*, *.e2e.*, *.integration.*, and files under __tests__/), where dynamic loading is sometimes required by test utilities.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// Static import at the top of the file
import { parseConfig } from './config-parser';

// Allowed in test files: mymodule.test.ts
const module = await import('./module');
import('./module').then((m) => m.default);
const pkg = require('./package');

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect (in non-test files)
docs.text:
// In mymodule.ts
const module = await import('./heavy-module');
import('./heavy-module').then((m) => m.default);

const pkg = require('some-package');

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-dynamic-import': 'error'

docs.title: no-empty-catch
docs.text: Disallow empty catch blocks that silently swallow errors.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: An empty catch block discards the error entirely. The caller has no indication that anything went wrong, diagnostics are impossible, and bugs become untraceable. Every caught error must be handled in some meaningful way: logged, re-thrown, returned as a result, or surfaced to the user.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
try {
  riskyOperation();
} catch (err) {
  logger.error('riskyOperation failed', err);
}

try {
  connectToDb();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error(`Database connection failed: ${err}`);
}

try {
  cleanup();
} catch {
  throw new Error('Cleanup step failed');
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
try {
  riskyOperation();
} catch (err) {}

try {
  connectToDb();
} catch {}

try {
  cleanup();
} catch (err) {
} finally {
  teardown();
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-empty-catch': 'error'

docs.title: no-eslint-disable
docs.text: Prevent use of eslint-disable comments; fix the underlying issue instead.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
eslint-disable comments suppress rule violations rather than fixing them. They accumulate over time, making it impossible to know whether a rule violation is intentional or forgotten. A zero-tolerance codebase should have no suppression comments: every violation should be fixed at its source.

Flagged comment forms:

  • // eslint-disable
  • // eslint-disable-next-line
  • // eslint-disable-line
  • /* eslint-disable */ block comments

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// Fix the underlying issue instead of disabling the rule
const MAX_SIZE = 100;
if (items.length > MAX_SIZE) {
  throw new Error('Too many items');
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
// eslint-disable-next-line zero-tolerance/no-magic-numbers
if (items.length > 100) {
  /* ... */
}

/* eslint-disable zero-tolerance/no-throw-literal */
throw 'something went wrong';
/* eslint-enable zero-tolerance/no-throw-literal */

docs.title: no-explicit-any
docs.text: Disallow explicit any.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: any turns off the type system exactly where code is most likely to drift. If a value is unknown, model it as unknown and narrow it deliberately, or define a real domain type.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
const payload: unknown = input;

function identity<T>(value: T): T {
  return value;
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect

  return String(value);
}

docs.title: no-export-alias
docs.text: Prevent use of aliases in export statements; export values under their original names.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Export aliases (export { foo as bar }) create a disconnect between the internal name of a value and the name that consumers use. This makes it harder to search for a symbol across the codebase and increases the chance of confusion. Export the value directly, or rename it at the declaration site.

docs.title: Autofix
docs.text: This rule intentionally does not autofix true public aliases such as export { foo as bar }, because correcting them safely requires a naming decision. Redundant same-name exports are already valid syntax and are not reported as aliases.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
export { fetchUser };
export { createOrder };
export { validateSchema };

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect

docs.title: no-fetch-in-tests
docs.text: Disallow fetch usage in test files.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended off Strict off

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Direct HTTP calls in tests create network-dependent failures and blur the boundary between unit, integration, and end-to-end testing. Prefer injecting a client, using a mock transport, or keeping real HTTP behind explicit integration-test helpers.

This rule is opt-in and disabled by default in the built-in presets. It only runs in recognized test files: *.test.*, *.spec.*, *.e2e.*, *.integration.*, and files under __tests__/.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
const client = createMockClient({
  '/users/1': { id: '1', name: 'Ada' },
});

await loadUser(client, '1');

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect

await fetch('/users/1');
await globalThis.fetch('/users/1');
await window.fetch('/users/1');

This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-fetch-in-tests': 'error'

docs.title: no-flag-argument
docs.text: Disallow boolean flag parameters in function signatures.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Boolean flag arguments usually indicate a function doing more than one thing. Prefer explicit methods, a command object, or a parameter object (Remove Flag Argument, Introduce Parameter Object, Replace Function with Command).

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
function renderPreview(): string {
  return 'preview';
}

function renderFull(): string {
  return 'full';
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:

  return isPreview ? 'preview' : 'full';

docs.title: no-floating-promises
docs.text: Disallow unhandled promise expressions. Promise-producing expressions must be explicitly handled with await, void, .catch(...), or then(..., onRejected).

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Floating promises frequently hide failures and create non-deterministic behavior. This rule enforces explicit handling so async intent is visible and rejected promises are not silently ignored.

The rule checks explicit promise-producing patterns such as:

  • dynamic import(...)
  • new Promise(...)
  • async IIFE calls ((async () => ...)())
  • promise chains using .then(...), .catch(...), and .finally(...)
  • Promise static calls such as Promise.resolve(...) and Promise.all(...)

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
await import('./worker');

void bootstrapAsync();

fetchData().catch(handleError);

fetchData().then(handleData, handleError);

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
import('./worker');

Promise.resolve(42);

(async () => {
  await bootstrapAsync();
})();

fetchData().then(handleData);

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-floating-promises': 'error'

docs.title: Behavioral contract
docs.text:
The rule resolves stable local async function declarations and initialized async arrows by lexical binding. A synchronous parameter or local declaration with the same name is respected, and bindings are never carried between files. Async generators return iterators and are not treated as promises. When TypeScript parser services are available, promise-returning external calls and promise-valued expressions are checked too. Without those services, unknown external return types and aliases remain outside the syntactic check.

A rejection callback must appear on the terminal call. .catch(handleError).then(work) and .catch(handleError).finally(cleanup) produce new promises that need handling. Missing, null, or undefined callbacks are not handlers. Inline callbacks that visibly rethrow, return Promise.reject, or are async also require handling. Arbitrary callback references are accepted as explicit intent; the rule does not prove that their implementations cannot throw.

docs.title: no-for-in
docs.text: Report for..in loops, which visit inherited enumerable keys.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Object.keys visits only own enumerable keys, while for..in also visits inherited enumerable keys. The rule reports the loop without rewriting it so the author can choose the intended iteration behavior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: for (const key in record) { handle(key); } is reported. for (const key of Object.keys(record)) { handle(key); } is allowed. If inherited keys are required, review the rule setting for that code.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/no-for-in': 'error'

docs.title: no-hardcoded-secrets
docs.text: Disallow hardcoded secrets, credentials, tokens, and secret-looking env defaults.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Credentials committed to source code are difficult to rotate and can expose production systems. Read secrets from managed configuration and avoid literal fallbacks.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
const token = process.env.API_TOKEN;

const fixture = 'dummy-secret-token';

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
const apiKey = 'sk_live_12345678901234567890';

const databaseUrl = 'postgres://user:password@database.internal/db';

const token = process.env.API_TOKEN ?? '12345678901234567890';

'zero-tolerance/no-hardcoded-secrets': ['error', {
  allowedPatterns: ['test-', 'dummy', 'example', 'fake', 'placeholder'],
  minimumSecretLength: 16,

docs.title: no-identical-branches
docs.text: Disallow identical branches in conditionals.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: If both branches of an if/else or ternary expression are identical, the condition is unnecessary noise. Consolidate shared logic (Consolidate Duplicate Conditional Fragments) and simplify the code.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
if (enabled) {
  runFastPath();
} else {
  runSafePath();
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
if (enabled) {
  execute();
} else {
  execute();
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-identical-branches': 'error'

docs.title: no-identical-expressions
docs.text:
Find likely copy-and-paste mistakes in comparisons and logical expressions.

Type: problem. No automatic fix. No options.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text: Reports repeated identifiers or primitive literals on both sides of ===, !==, ==, !=, &&, ||, or ??. Parentheses and comments do not hide a repeated identifier. Primitive literals include strings, numbers, booleans, null, and bigints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
const fallback = value || value; // Reported: repeats the same value.
const doubled = text + text; // Allowed: arithmetic may be intentional.
const same = next() === next(); // Allowed: calls may return different values.
const equal = /item/ === /item/; // Allowed: creates two separate objects.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Calls, property reads, updates, and compound expressions are excluded because evaluating them can have effects. This includes optional calls, computed properties, and getters. Comparing the same regular-expression variable with itself is still reported.

A diagnostic asks you to review the expression; it does not prove that the result is constant. For example, self-comparison may intentionally test for NaN. There is no automatic fix because the intended replacement is unknown.

docs.title: no-indexed-access-types
docs.text: Disallow TypeScript indexed access types (T["key"], T[K], T[number]).

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Indexed access types expose the internal structure of another type and make refactors brittle. They also hide intent at the usage site because the reader has to mentally resolve the referenced property or element shape.

Prefer extracting and naming the contract you actually want to use.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text: By default the rule reports only. When configured with aliasNamePattern, it can suggest extracting the indexed access to a generated top-level type alias and replacing the usage with that alias. Supported placeholders are {object}, {property}, and {index}; generated names are sanitized to PascalCase and refused when they collide with an existing top-level binding.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
type UserName = string;

interface IUserSummary {
  name: UserName;
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect

type Item = (typeof things)['items'][0];

docs.text:
This rule accepts an optional alias name pattern for suggestions:

'zero-tolerance/no-indexed-access-types': ['error', { aliasNamePattern: '{object}{property}' }]

docs.title: no-inline-type-import

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable Yes Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Inline type import queries make dependencies harder to scan and enforce inconsistently across files. Requiring top-level import type statements keeps imports explicit, grouped, and easier to maintain.

docs.title: Autofix
docs.text: Simple import("module").Name references are fixed by replacing the inline reference with Name and adding or reusing a top-level import type declaration. The fixer refuses cases where the generated type name would collide with an existing top-level binding.

docs.title: no-jest-have-been-called
docs.text: Require explicit call counts and invocation indices in Jest expect(...) assertions. Negated toHaveBeenCalled and toBeCalled assertions are allowed because they assert zero calls.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
toHaveBeenCalled / toBeCalled only asserts that a mock was called at least once without specifying how many times. toHaveBeenCalledWith / toBeCalledWith does not specify which invocation is being checked. toHaveBeenLastCalledWith / toLastCalledWith implicitly asserts only the final invocation, silently ignoring all others. All of these matchers can pass for the wrong reasons, producing false confidence.

The negated not.toHaveBeenCalled() and not.toBeCalled() forms assert exactly zero calls, so the rule allows them.

Using toHaveBeenCalledTimes(n) forces you to declare the exact call count. Using toHaveBeenNthCalledWith(n, ...args) forces you to assert the arguments for a specific invocation. Together they produce precise, non-ambiguous test assertions.

The rule checks calls on expect(...), globalThis.expect(...), and global.expect(...), including aliases imported from @jest/globals. It follows not, resolves, and rejects modifiers. A same-named method on an unrelated object, or a matcher property read without a call, is allowed.

Banned Replacement toHaveBeenCalled toHaveBeenCalledTimes toBeCalled toHaveBeenCalledTimes toHaveBeenCalledWith toHaveBeenNthCalledWith toBeCalledWith toHaveBeenNthCalledWith toHaveBeenLastCalledWith toHaveBeenNthCalledWith toLastCalledWith toHaveBeenNthCalledWith

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenNthCalledWith(1, 'expected-argument');

expect(mockFn).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenCalled();
expect(mockFn).toBeCalled();

expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenCalledWith('expected-argument');
expect(mockFn).toBeCalledWith('expected-argument');

expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenLastCalledWith('expected-argument');
expect(mockFn).toLastCalledWith('expected-argument');

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-jest-have-been-called': 'error'

docs.title: Parsing and fix safety
docs.text: Object prototype properties, including optional and bracket access to toString, valueOf, and constructor, are allowed. Async, computed, and optional banned matcher calls remain reported when they belong to a Jest assertion. Negated argument matchers such as not.toHaveBeenCalledWith(...) remain reported.

docs.title: no-labels
docs.text: Disallow labeled statements.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Labels introduce goto-like control flow (break label, continue label) that makes code harder to follow and maintain. Prefer extracting logic into functions or using clearer loop structures.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
for (const row of rows) {
  if (!row.valid) {
    break;
  }
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
outer: for (const row of rows) {
  for (const cell of row.cells) {
    if (!cell.valid) {
      break outer;
    }
  }
}
