docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-labels': 'error'

docs.title: no-literal-property-unions
docs.text: Require property literal unions to use named domain types.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Property contracts that use literal unions hide finite or constrained domains inside object shapes. Defining the domain as a named type gives the allowed values a reusable name and keeps interface, type literal, and class property declarations from repeating raw values.

For string and number domains, prefer an enum. Bigint literal unions are allowed because TypeScript enums cannot represent bigint values, and there is no universally accepted lightweight pattern to replace them.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
enum SearchMode {
  TreeSitter = 'tree-sitter',
  RipgrepPrefilter = 'ripgrep-prefilter',
  TextHint = 'text-hint',
}

export interface IAstLangSearchMatch {
  path: string;
  line: number;
  column: number;
  text: string;
  matchedTerm: string;
  mode: SearchMode;
}

enum ExitCode {
  Success = 0,
  Failure = 1,
}

interface IProcessResult {
  exitCode: ExitCode;
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
export interface IAstLangSearchMatch {
  path: string;
  line: number;
  column: number;
  text: string;
  matchedTerm: string;
  mode: 'tree-sitter' | 'ripgrep-prefilter' | 'text-hint';
}

interface IProcessResult {
  exitCode: 0 | 1;
}

type SearchMatch = {
  mode: 'tree-sitter' | 'text-hint' | undefined;
};

interface ISearchMatch {
  slug: `a-${string}` | `b-${string}`;
}

interface ISearchMatch {
  mode: 'tree-sitter' | string;
}

interface ISearchMatch {
  value: true | 'yes';
}

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This rule checks interface property signatures, type literal property signatures, class properties, and abstract class properties. It ignores function parameters and type aliases because those are covered by no-literal-unions.

Pure boolean property unions (true | false) are allowed because they represent the full boolean domain and do not benefit from a named domain. Bigint literal unions are also allowed because TypeScript enums cannot represent bigint values. Literal unions mixed with non-boolean members, widened types, or nullish members are still reported.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-literal-property-unions': 'error'

docs.title: no-literal-unions
docs.text: Ban literal union types in favour of enums.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Literal union types ("active" | "inactive") scatter magic values throughout the codebase, are not refactor-safe, and provide no single place to enumerate valid values. The same problem exists when a type alias hides those values behind typeof references to same-file literal-valued const declarations. TypeScript enums give string and number domains a canonical home, making them easy to discover, iterate over, and refactor.

Property declarations are handled by no-literal-property-unions, which reports on the property name and keeps property value domains separate from general type aliases and parameters.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
enum Status {
  Active = 'active',
  Inactive = 'inactive',
}

enum Direction {
  North,
  South,
  East,
  West,
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
type Status = 'active' | 'inactive';

type Direction = 'north' | 'south' | 'east' | 'west';

type Size = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' | 'xl';

const ACTIVE = 'active';
const INACTIVE = 'inactive';

type Status = typeof ACTIVE | typeof INACTIVE;

const DEFAULT_STATUS = `default`;

type StatusName = typeof DEFAULT_STATUS | 'custom';

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Pure boolean unions (true | false) are exempt because they represent the full boolean domain and do not benefit from an enum:

// ✅ Allowed — exhaustive boolean union
type Toggle = true | false;

The same exemption applies when a type alias references same-file boolean literal const declarations:

const ENABLED = true;
const DISABLED = false;

type Toggle = typeof ENABLED | typeof DISABLED;

Literal unions inside built-in TypeScript utility types are also exempt because they commonly describe property keys, filters, or type transformations rather than enum domains:

// Allowed: property-key selection
type PublicUser = Omit<User, 'password' | 'token'>;
type NamedUser = Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>;
type UsersByRole = Record<'admin' | 'guest', User>;

// Allowed: utility filtering and transformation
type NonDraftStatus = Exclude<Status, 'draft' | 'archived'>;
type VisibleStatus = Extract<Status, 'published' | 'scheduled'>;
type RequiredStatus = NonNullable<'active' | 'inactive' | null>;

The utility-type exemption is limited to known TypeScript utility types. Custom generics are still checked:

// Still reported
type WrappedStatus = CustomUtility<'active' | 'inactive'>;

docs.title: Migration safety
docs.text: This rule reports without an autofix. Replacing a string literal union with an enum changes assignability, emits runtime code, and can introduce a value binding that collides with an existing declaration. A migration must update callers and literal values across the project. For example, a value previously assigned as "active" must become Status.Active.

docs.title: no-magic-numbers
docs.text: Disallow raw numeric literals in expressions; use named constants instead.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Magic numbers are numeric literals that appear without explanation. They make code hard to read (what does 86400 mean?) and hard to maintain (every occurrence must be updated if the value changes). Extracting them into named constants adds meaning and creates a single source of truth.

Allowed values: 0, 1, and -1 are universally understood and are always permitted.

Allowed locations:

  • const variable initialisers — this is how you define a named constant
  • TypeScript enum member values

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
const SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400;
const MAX_RETRIES = 3;
const HTTP_OK = 200;

// Allowed sentinel values
const index = -1;
const first = arr[0];
const length = arr.length + 1;

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
setTimeout(callback, 86400 * 1000);

if (response.status === 200) {
  /* ... */
}

let retries = 3; // let or var declaration — not a named const

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-magic-numbers': 'error'

docs.title: no-magic-strings
docs.text: Disallow magic string literals in comparisons and switch-case clauses; use named constants instead.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
String literals used in comparisons (=== 'admin') or switch cases are magic strings: their meaning is implicit, they can be mis-typed silently, and every occurrence must be updated if the value changes. Defining them as named constants (const ROLE_ADMIN = 'admin') adds meaning and creates a single source of truth.

Checked locations:

  • ===, !==, ==, != binary comparisons
  • switch case test values

typeof comparisons are exempt (for example, typeof value === 'string').

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
const ROLE_ADMIN = 'admin';
const STATUS_ACTIVE = 'active';

if (user.role === ROLE_ADMIN) {
  /* ... */
}

switch (user.status) {
  case STATUS_ACTIVE:
    break;
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
if (user.role === 'admin') {
  /* ... */
}

switch (user.status) {
  case 'active':
    break;
  case 'inactive':
    break;
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule accepts an optional options object:

'zero-tolerance/no-magic-strings': [
  'error',
  {
    checkComparisons: true,
    checkSwitchCases: true,
    ignoreValues: ['production'],
  },
]

docs.title: no-map-set-mutation
docs.text: Disallow direct Map and Set mutation methods.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Mutable Map and Set instances are the same shortcut as mutating arrays and objects in place. Rebuilding a collection makes state transitions explicit and easier to reason about.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
const cache = new Map<string, number>();
const answer = cache.get('answer');

const ids = new Set<string>();
const hasId = ids.has('abc');

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
const cache = new Map<string, number>();
cache.set('answer', 42);

const ids = new Set<string>();
ids.add('abc');

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-map-set-mutation': 'error'

docs.title: Type Information
docs.text: This rule relies on typed linting so it can distinguish real Map and Set instances from unrelated objects that happen to expose similarly named methods.

docs.title: no-math-random
docs.text: Disallow Math.random().

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Ad hoc randomness makes behavior non-deterministic and difficult to test. Reading randomness through an injected generator or boundary keeps behavior explicit and reproducible.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
const value = rng.nextFloat();

const rounded = Math.round(value);

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
const value = Math.random();

const id = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10);

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-math-random': 'error'

docs.title: no-mock-implementation
docs.text: Prohibit persistent mock setup methods; use their Once variants to prevent test bleeds.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
mockImplementation, mockReturnValue, mockResolvedValue, and mockRejectedValue configure a mock persistently for the lifetime of the test suite (or until manually reset). This means a mock configured in one test silently bleeds into subsequent tests, leading to hard-to-diagnose ordering-dependent failures.

The Once variants (mockImplementationOnce, mockReturnValueOnce, mockResolvedValueOnce, mockRejectedValueOnce) only apply for a single call and then revert. This eliminates the source of test bleeds entirely.

Banned Replacement mockImplementation mockImplementationOnce mockReturnValue mockReturnValueOnce mockResolvedValue mockResolvedValueOnce mockRejectedValue mockRejectedValueOnce

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
jest.fn().mockImplementationOnce(() => 'value');
jest.fn().mockReturnValueOnce(42);
jest.fn().mockResolvedValueOnce({ data: 'ok' });
jest.fn().mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('failed'));

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
jest.fn().mockImplementation(() => 'value');
jest.fn().mockReturnValue(42);
jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ data: 'ok' });
jest.fn().mockRejectedValue(new Error('failed'));

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-mock-implementation': 'error'

docs.title: Parsing and fix safety
docs.text: Object prototype properties, including optional and bracket access to toString, valueOf, and constructor, are allowed. Only explicit banned names match the replacement map.

docs.title: no-non-null-assertion
docs.text: Disallow non-null assertions using the ! postfix operator.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The ! postfix operator tells TypeScript to treat an expression as non-null without any runtime check. If the value is actually null or undefined at runtime, the assertion causes a crash rather than a handled error. Use optional chaining (?.), nullish coalescing (??), or an explicit null check instead.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text: The rule offers optional-chaining suggestions for safe member and call forms such as value!.prop, value![key], and value!(). Suggestions are withheld for assignment/update targets and other contexts where optional chaining would change behavior or require a larger rewrite.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// Optional chaining
const name = user?.profile?.name;

// Nullish coalescing
const displayName = user?.name ?? 'Anonymous';

// Explicit null check
if (element !== null) {
  element.focus();
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
const name = user!.profile!.name;

document.getElementById('root')!.innerHTML = '';

const value = maybeNull!;

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-non-null-assertion': 'error'

docs.title: no-object-mutation
docs.text: Disallow direct object-property mutation.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Mutating object properties in place introduces side effects and makes state transitions harder to trace. Immutable updates improve predictability.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
const next = { ...state, count: state.count + 1 };

class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message: string, context?: Record<string, unknown>) {
    super(message);
    this.name = this.constructor.name;
    this.context = context;
  }
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text: state.count = state.count + 1;

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/no-object-mutation': 'error'

docs.title: no-parameter-reassign
docs.text: Disallow assignments and updates to function parameters.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Reassigning parameters is a common code smell that makes control flow harder to follow and hides intent. Prefer introducing a new local variable (Extract Variable / Split Variable) instead of mutating the input parameter.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
function normalize(value: string): string {
  let normalized = value.trim();
  normalized = normalized.toLowerCase();
  return normalized;
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
function normalize(value: string): string {
  value = value.trim();
  value = value.toLowerCase();
  return value;
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-parameter-reassign': 'error'

docs.title: Parsing and fix safety
docs.text: The rule resolves parameter bindings through ESLint scope analysis. It detects writes from closures, destructured bindings, and destructuring assignments while allowing writes to shadowing local variables.

docs.title: no-parent-internal-access
docs.text: Disallow parent-relative access into protected internal directories such as src.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended off Strict off

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Parent-relative paths like ../src/... and ../../src/... usually mean one module is reaching into another module's internal implementation instead of consuming its public entrypoint. That creates tight coupling, makes refactors harder, and breaks the expectation that protected directories such as src, app, or internal are self-contained boundaries.

This rule is opt-in and disabled by default in the built-in presets.

By default, the rule protects the src directory name. You can override that list with the protectedDirectories option.

Matching is intentionally narrow:

  • only parent-relative paths are checked
  • only the first concrete directory reached after .. traversal is matched
  • protectedDirectories entries are trimmed, deduplicated, and empty entries are ignored

This rule checks:

  • import ... from '...'
  • import('...')
  • require('...')
  • TypeScript import x = require('...')
  • direct re-exports such as export { x } from '...' and export * from '...'

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
import { feature } from '../shared/feature';
import localFeature from './src/local-feature';
export { childFeature } from './src/child-feature';
import { nestedFeature } from '../shared/src/feature';

import { parentValue } from '../parent';
const localValue = parentValue;
export { localValue };

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
import { feature } from '../src/feature';
const legacyFeature = require('../../src/legacy-feature');
const dynamicFeature = await import('../src/dynamic-feature');
import feature = require('../src/feature');

export { sharedFeature } from '../src/shared-feature';
export * from '../../src/shared-feature';

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Default configuration:

'zero-tolerance/no-parent-internal-access': 'error'

Custom protected directory names:

'zero-tolerance/no-parent-internal-access': [
  'error',
  {
    protectedDirectories: ['src', 'app', 'internal'],
  },
]

This matches ../src/foo and ../../app/foo, but not ../shared/src/foo because shared is the first traversed directory.

docs.title: no-placeholder-implementation
docs.text: Disallow placeholder, stub, TODO, and not implemented production code.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Placeholder implementations often compile while silently dropping behavior. Production code should either implement the path or fail through an explicit reviewed design.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
function find(value: string): string | null {
  if (value.length === 0) {
    return null;
  }
  return value;
}

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
function load(): never {
  throw new Error('TODO');
}

function build(): object {
  return {};
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-placeholder-implementation': ['error', {
  checkComments: true,
  checkTests: false,
  allowedTerms: []
}]

docs.title: no-process-env-outside-config
docs.text: Disallow process.env reads outside configuration modules.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Scattered process.env reads create hidden dependencies and inconsistent configuration behavior. Read environment variables once in configuration modules, validate them there, and import typed config values elsewhere.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// src/config.ts
export const mode = process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development';

// src/app.ts
import { mode } from './config';

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
const mode = process.env.NODE_ENV;

const { NODE_ENV } = process.env;

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options. process.env is allowed in files under /config/ and in filenames such as config.ts, env.ts, and vite.config.ts:

'zero-tolerance/no-process-env-outside-config': 'error'

docs.title: no-query-side-effects
docs.text:
Keep query functions from changing shared state while allowing local calculations.

Type: suggestion. No automatic fix. No options.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Checks function names that start with get, is, has, can, or should followed by an uppercase letter or underscore, such as getUser and is_ready.

Reports assignments, updates, deletes, and recognized mutating method calls that affect arguments, outer variables, this, or shared objects. Optional calls and static computed property names follow the same checks.

Local variables may be reassigned. Direct writes to fresh local arrays and objects are allowed, including containers declared with TypeScript assertions. Rebinding a parameter is local; changing an object passed as a parameter is shared mutation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
function getItems() {
  const items = [] as number[];
  items.push(1); // Allowed: builds a fresh local result.
  return items;
}

function getUser(user) {
  user.visits++; // Reported: changes the caller's object.
  return user;
}

docs.title: When a local object becomes shared
docs.text:
Passing an object to another function, creating an alias, or capturing it in a closure can expose it outside the query. Later writes are checked. If a loop reuses and exposes the same object, writes on later iterations are also checked. A new object created inside each iteration can still be built locally before it is exposed.

Writes through getters or setters remain checked because they may change shared state. Nested property writes also remain checked: a fresh outer object can contain shared inner objects. Casting a shared object does not make it local.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The rule does not inspect the bodies of arbitrary called functions. Method names are used to recognize likely mutations. Each nested function is checked in its own scope. Other immutability rules may reject local mutations that this rule allows.

docs.title: no-raw-sql-interpolation
docs.text: Disallow interpolated raw SQL and unsafe raw query helpers.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: SQL strings built with interpolation or concatenation are injection-prone. Use parameterized calls or an approved tagged query builder.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
db.query('select * from users where id = ?', [id]);

sql`select * from users where id = ${id}`;

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
db.query(`select * from users where id = ${id}`);

db.execute('delete from users where id = ' + id);

prisma.$queryRawUnsafe('select * from users');

Calls without arguments and calls that spread their first argument do not report interpolation. A diagnostic points to the interpolated argument only after it has been validated.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-raw-sql-interpolation': ['error', {
  allowedTags: ['sql', 'Prisma.sql', 'db.sql'],
  additionalSinkNames: []
}]

docs.title: no-re-export
docs.text: Disallow direct and pass-through re-export statements from parent or ancestor modules in non-barrel files.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (code) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Re-export statements that reach outside the current directory (../) create upward dependencies that violate proper module hierarchy. That includes direct re-exports such as export { foo } from '../foo' and pass-through patterns such as import { foo } from '../foo'; export { foo };. Statement ordering does not matter: export { foo }; import { foo } from '../foo'; is also reported. Barrel files (index.*) remain exempt from this rule because their re-export path policy is enforced separately by require-barrel-relative-exports. All other files must not re-export from peer modules (../sibling) or ancestors (../../parent, ../../../grandparent).

docs.title: Autofix
docs.text: The fixer only removes redundant pass-through export specifiers when the same exported name is already directly exported from the same file. Parent-path re-export statements and non-redundant pass-through exports remain report-only.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The barrel-file exemption applies only to single-extension index files such as index.ts, index.js, and index.mts.
  • Double-extension files such as index.d.ts, index.test.ts, and index.spec.js are not treated as barrel files and are still checked by this rule.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// Direct exports
export { foo, bar };
export const value = 42;
export function myFunction() {}

// Re-exports from children (always allowed)
export { childFunction } from './child';
export * from './child/utils';

// Exporting a local binding remains allowed
import { parentValue } from '../parent';
const localValue = parentValue;
export { localValue };

// In a barrel file, this rule stays silent because
// require-barrel-relative-exports owns barrel re-export path policy.

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
// Re-exports from peers are not allowed in non-barrel files
export { peerFunction } from '../sibling';
export * from '../utils';

// Re-exports from parents are not allowed
export { parentFunction } from '../../parent';
export * from '../../grandparent';

// Pass-through re-exports from parents are also not allowed
import { peerFunction } from '../sibling';
export { peerFunction };

import parentDefault from '../../parent';
export default parentDefault;

// Re-exports from grandparents are not allowed
export { grandparentFunction } from '../../../ancestor';
export * as ns from '../../../../distant-ancestor';

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-re-export': 'error'

docs.title: no-redundant-boolean
docs.text: Simplify comparisons and ternaries only when their boolean result is preserved.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (code) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: A strict comparison such as value === true cannot safely become value unless the operand is known to be boolean: 1 === true is false, while 1 is truthy. This rule only simplifies comparisons whose operand is syntactically boolean. A ternary such as condition ? true : false becomes !!condition when the condition's type is unknown, preserving the boolean result. Removing !! keeps the inner expression parenthesized so surrounding arithmetic and unary operators retain their precedence. Expressions containing comments are left unchanged.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: (value > 0) === true is reported and fixed to value > 0. condition ? true : false is fixed to !!condition. 1 + !!(value > 0) is fixed to 1 + (value > 0). value === true is allowed when value is not syntactically known to be boolean.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/no-redundant-boolean': 'error'

docs.title: no-restricted-imports-in-tests
docs.text: Disallow configured dependency imports in test files.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended off Strict off

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Tests should make expensive boundaries explicit. Directly importing filesystem, process, and network modules inside test files often leads to tests that depend on local machine state, real sockets, subprocesses, or external services. This rule is opt-in so projects can adopt it where those boundaries matter most.

By default, the rule restricts these module roots in test files:

axios, child_process, dgram, dns, fs, got, http, http2, https, net, node-fetch, tls, undici, worker_threads

The node: protocol is normalized before matching, so node:fs, node:fs/promises, and fs/promises all match the fs root. Entries ending in /* are also normalized, so configured values such as fs/* and node:fs/* protect the same root.

This rule checks:

  • import ... from '...'
  • import('...')
  • require('...')
  • TypeScript import x = require('...')
  • direct re-exports such as export { x } from '...' and export * from '...'

It only runs in recognized test files: *.test.*, *.spec.*, *.e2e.*, *.integration.*, and files under __tests__/.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
import { createFixture } from './fixtures';
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';

const client = createMockClient();
const result = await runScenario(client);

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
import fs from 'fs';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { execFile } from 'node:child_process';
import axios from 'axios';

const http = require('http');
const net = await import('node:net');
import workerThreads = require('node:worker_threads');

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Default configuration:

'zero-tolerance/no-restricted-imports-in-tests': 'error'

Custom restricted module roots:

'zero-tolerance/no-restricted-imports-in-tests': [
  'error',
  {
    modules: ['fs', 'node:fs/*', 'child_process', 'axios', '@company/database'],
  },
]

Configured module names are trimmed, lowercased, normalized by removing node:, and matched by module root. For example, fs matches fs, fs/promises, node:fs, and node:fs/promises.

docs.title: no-return-type
docs.text: Disallow TypeScript ReturnType utility usage.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
ReturnType<typeof fn> couples consumers to a function's implementation details instead of an explicit, named contract. When the function's return type changes, dependent types change silently too.

Prefer declaring a named result type and making that contract explicit.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text: When ReturnType<typeof fn> references a same-file function declaration or const function with an explicit return annotation, the rule suggests replacing ReturnType<typeof fn> with that annotation text. Other cases remain report-only.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
type FetchResult = { data: IUser; status: number };

async function fetchUser(): Promise<FetchResult> {
  // ...
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text: type FetchUserResult = ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>;

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-return-type': 'error'

docs.title: no-set-interval-in-tests
docs.text: Disallow setInterval usage in test files.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Intervals in tests create background work that can leak across assertions, suites, or worker lifetimes. Prefer fake timers, direct event triggering, or a test helper that exposes a deterministic signal.

This rule only runs in recognized test files: *.test.*, *.spec.*, *.e2e.*, *.integration.*, and files under __tests__/.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
vi.useFakeTimers();

const subscription = startPolling();
vi.advanceTimersByTime(1000);
subscription.stop();

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
setInterval(poll, 1000);
global.setInterval(poll, 1000);
window.setInterval(poll, 1000);

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-set-interval-in-tests': 'error'

docs.title: no-set-timeout-in-tests
docs.text: Disallow setTimeout usage in test files.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Real-time sleeps make tests slower and timing-dependent. A passing test can still be waiting longer than necessary, while a failing test may only fail under CI load or on slower machines. Prefer fake timers, explicit async coordination, or framework polling helpers that wait for an observable condition.

This rule only runs in recognized test files: *.test.*, *.spec.*, *.e2e.*, *.integration.*, and files under __tests__/.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
vi.useFakeTimers();

const pending = promiseUnderTest();
vi.advanceTimersByTime(100);
await pending;

await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('Done')).toBeVisible());

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
setTimeout(assertLater, 100);
globalThis.setTimeout(assertLater, 100);
window.setTimeout(assertLater, 100);

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-set-timeout-in-tests': 'error'

docs.title: no-shell-command-construction
docs.text: Disallow shell command construction through subprocess APIs.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Shell command strings are hard to quote safely and can become OS command injection sinks. Prefer executable plus argument-vector APIs or a reviewed wrapper.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
spawn('git', ['status']);

execFile('git', ['status']);

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
exec(command);

spawn(`git ${cmd}`, []);

spawn('git', ['status'], { shell: true });

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-shell-command-construction': ['error', {
  approvedWrapperNames: [],
  additionalShellFunctionNames: []
}]

docs.title: no-sinon-imprecise-spy-assertions
docs.text: Require explicit call counts and numbered-call argument checks in Sinon assertions.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
sinon.assert.called(spy) only requires one or more calls. The calledWith variants match any invocation when passed the whole spy. Use callCount(spy, n) for an exact count and pass spy.getCall(index) to an argument assertion when a particular invocation matters.

The rule recognizes default, namespace, and named assert imports from sinon, including aliases and computed method names. notCalled, calledOnce, and calledOnceWithExactly are allowed because their counts are explicit.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
import sinon from 'sinon';

sinon.assert.callCount(spy, 2);
sinon.assert.calledWithExactly(spy.getCall(0), 'first');
sinon.assert.notCalled(spy);

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
import sinon from 'sinon';

sinon.assert.called(spy);
sinon.assert.calledWith(spy, 'first');
sinon.assert.calledWithExactly(spy, 'first');

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-sinon-imprecise-spy-assertions': 'error'

This rule applies regardless of the test runner, including Mocha. It checks sinon.assert calls rather than arbitrary spy methods or properties.

docs.title: no-test-interface-declaration
docs.text: Disallow interface declarations in test files; import production types instead.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Declaring an interface inside a test file is almost always a sign that the production code is not exporting a proper type contract. When a test author creates a local interface to type mock objects or fixtures, that type drifts independently from the real production shape. If the production type changes, the test's copy won't break, silently hiding regressions.

The correct fix is to define the interface in the production module and import it in the test.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// user.ts (production)
export interface IUser {
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

// user.test.ts
import type { IUser } from './user';

const mockUser: IUser = { name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' };

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
// user.test.ts
interface IUser {
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

const mockUser: IUser = { name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' };

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-test-interface-declaration': 'error'

docs.title: no-throw-literal
docs.text: Disallow throwing literals, plain objects, or template strings; always throw a new Error() instance.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Only Error instances (and subclasses) include a stack trace. Throwing a string, object, number, or template literal discards diagnostic information and can break error-handling code that expects an Error.

By default, this rule only allows:

  • throw new ... expressions (for example throw new Error(...))
  • re-throwing the active catch parameter (for example catch (err) { throw err; })

You can opt into allowing throw <call>, throw <member>, and throw await <expr> with rule options.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
throw new Error('something went wrong');

throw new TypeError('expected a string');

throw new RangeError('value out of range');

class ValidationError extends Error {}
throw new ValidationError('invalid input');

// Re-throwing a caught error
try {
  riskyOp();
} catch (err) {
  throw err;
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
throw 'something went wrong';

throw 404;

throw { message: 'error', code: 500 };

throw `failed: ${reason}`;

throw condition ? 'error-a' : 'error-b';

throw createError('message');

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule accepts an optional options object:

'zero-tolerance/no-throw-literal': [
  'error',
  {
    allowThrowingCallExpressions: false,
    allowThrowingMemberExpressions: false,
    allowThrowingAwaitExpressions: false,
  },
]

docs.title: no-ts-nocheck
docs.text: Prevent use of @ts-nocheck comments.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: @ts-nocheck disables TypeScript diagnostics for an entire file. That hides type errors at the file boundary and allows unsafe code to accumulate. Fix the underlying type errors instead of turning the checker off.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// @ts-expect-error intentional negative test for a public type
const value: string = 1;

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
// @ts-nocheck
const value: string = 1;

/* @ts-nocheck */
const otherValue: number = 'wrong';

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-ts-nocheck': 'error'

docs.title: no-type-assertion
docs.text: Prevent use of TypeScript type assertions (as and angle-bracket assertions) outside of test files.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Type assertions tell the TypeScript compiler to trust you over the type system. They are a common source of runtime errors because they bypass inference and structural checks. In production code, explicit type guards, generic functions, or proper data modelling should be used instead.

The rule allows as unknown and <unknown> in test files (.test.*, .spec.*, .e2e.*, .integration.*, and files under __tests__/) because this pattern is common in test utilities and rule tester setups.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text: For as assertions used directly as variable initializers, the rule suggests expr satisfies Type. Angle-bracket assertions and nested assertion expressions remain report-only because the rewrite is not always equivalent.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// Use a type guard instead
function isUser(value: unknown): value is IUser {
  return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && 'name' in value && 'email' in value;
}

// Generic function with a constraint
function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined {
  return arr[0];
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
const user = response.data as IUser;

const element = document.querySelector('#app') as HTMLDivElement;

const value = <MyType>getValue();

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-type-assertion': 'error'

docs.title: no-unawaited-async-assertion
docs.text: Require an asynchronous test assertion to be awaited or returned.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Jest promise matchers, Vitest polling and browser assertions, and Chai-as-promised assertions return a promise. Discarding that result can let a test finish before the assertion fails. The rule reports a direct assertion statement, including one prefixed with void, when the assertion promise is not awaited or returned.

It recognizes Jest and Vitest resolves and rejects; Vitest expect.poll and expect.element; Chai-as-promised eventually, rejected, fulfilled, rejectedWith, and become; and Chai's asynchronous assert methods. Imported aliases, local expect from a Vitest test callback, and static computed properties are supported. Chai-as-promised .notify(done) is allowed because the callback handles completion. The rule runs only in recognized test files.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
test('should resolve', async () => {
  await expect(load()).resolves.toBe('ready');
});

test('should reject', () => {
  return expect(load()).rejects.toThrow();
});

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
test('should resolve', () => {
  expect(load()).resolves.toBe('ready');
});

test('should find the element', () => {
  expect.poll(() => findElement()).toBeVisible();
});

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-unawaited-async-assertion': 'error'

The rule checks direct discarded assertion statements. Use a type-aware floating-promise rule to cover promises passed through variables or other expressions.

docs.title: no-unsafe-code-generation
docs.text: Disallow eval, Function constructors, string timers, and Node vm execution APIs.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Dynamic code execution expands injection risk and defeats static analysis. Prefer explicit functions, parsers, or constrained interpreters.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
setTimeout(() => run(), 100);

const value = parser.parse(source);

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
eval(source);

const fn = new Function(source);

setTimeout('run()', 100);

setInterval(`run(${value})`, 100);

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-unsafe-code-generation': 'error'

Direct timers are checked only when they resolve to unshadowed globals. Known global-object forms such as globalThis.setTimeout(...) are also checked, while arbitrary methods such as scheduler.setTimeout(...) are left alone.

docs.title: Parsing and fix safety
docs.text: Global eval and Function checks resolve direct identifiers and static members on unshadowed global objects. Unrelated methods with these names and dynamic computed keys are ignored.

docs.title: no-unsafe-json-parse
docs.text: Disallow treating JSON.parse results as typed data without validation.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Suggestions Yes Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: JSON.parse returns untrusted runtime data. Type assertions and annotations only change TypeScript's view of the value; they do not validate shape or content.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
const value: unknown = JSON.parse(input);

const config = ConfigSchema.parse(JSON.parse(input));

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
const config = JSON.parse(input) as Config;

const config: Config = JSON.parse(input);

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-unsafe-json-parse': ['error', {
  validatorNames: ['parse', 'safeParse', 'validate', 'assertValid'],
  allowedWrapperNames: ['safeJsonParse', 'parseJson']
}]

docs.title: no-vitest-imprecise-spy-assertions
docs.text: Require exact call counts and numbered invocation arguments in Vitest spy assertions.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
toHaveBeenCalled() proves only that a spy was called at least once. toHaveBeenCalledWith(...) can pass when any invocation matches, and toHaveBeenLastCalledWith(...) relies on an implicit last invocation. Use an exact count or a numbered call instead.

The rule recognizes expect imported from vitest, including aliases, expect.soft(...), computed matchers, and not, resolves, and rejects chains. not.toHaveBeenCalled() is allowed because it asserts zero calls, including after expect.soft(...). toHaveBeenCalledExactlyOnceWith(...) is also allowed.

docs.title: Correct
docs.text:
import { expect } from 'vitest';

expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
expect(spy).toHaveBeenNthCalledWith(1, 'first');
expect(spy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
expect.soft(spy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

docs.title: Incorrect
docs.text:
import { expect } from 'vitest';

expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalled();
expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('first');
expect(spy).toHaveBeenLastCalledWith('last');
expect.soft(spy).toHaveBeenCalled();

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/no-vitest-imprecise-spy-assertions': 'error'

The rule targets imported Vitest expect bindings. Global expect calls use Jest-compatible syntax and are covered by no-jest-have-been-called.

docs.title: no-with
docs.text: Disallow with statements.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type problem Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: with changes scope resolution rules in ways that are hard to reason about and optimize. It is disallowed in strict mode and should be replaced with explicit object property access.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text: const fullName = person.firstName + person.lastName;

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
with (person) {
  fullName = firstName + lastName;
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/no-with': 'error'

docs.title: prefer-guard-clauses
docs.text: Prefer guard clauses over else blocks after terminating if branches.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: When an if branch already returns or throws, keeping an else block adds unnecessary nesting. Flattening with guard clauses improves readability and aligns with Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
if (!user) {
  return;
}
processUser(user);

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
if (!user) {
  return;
} else {
  processUser(user);
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/prefer-guard-clauses': 'error'

docs.title: prefer-nullish-coalescing
docs.text: Prefer ?? for ternaries that repeat a locally bound identifier after a loose nullish check.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (code) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: value != null ? value : fallback can be shortened to a nullish coalescing expression when value is a declared local binding. The fixer parenthesizes the fallback to preserve the grouping of logical and conditional expressions. The rule skips unbound identifiers, which may resolve to global accessors. Member access, calls, and expressions containing comments are also left unchanged because rewriting them could change behavior or discard comments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For a locally declared value, value != null ? value : fallback && ready is reported and fixed to value ?? (fallback && ready). Repeated member access, calls, unbound identifiers, and commented expressions are allowed.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/prefer-nullish-coalescing': 'error'

docs.title: prefer-object-spread
docs.text: Report empty-target Object.assign calls for manual review.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended off Strict off

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Object.assign({}, source) and { ...source } can differ. Inlining an object literal getter preserves the getter instead of copying its current value. A source containing an own __proto__ key can also change the result's prototype under Object.assign. The rule is opt-in and does not autofix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Object.assign({}, source) is reported when the rule is enabled. { ...source } and Object.assign(target, source) are allowed. Review getters, setters, special keys, and any custom Object.assign binding before replacing a call.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/prefer-object-spread': 'warn'

docs.title: prefer-readonly-parameters
docs.text: Prefer readonly typing for object and array-like function parameters.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (--fix) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Function parameters are inputs. Treating object and array parameters as readonly prevents accidental mutation and preserves referential transparency.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
function format(user: Readonly<User>): string {
  return user.name;
}

function update(setName: Dispatch<SetStateAction<string>>): void {
  setName('ready');
}

class Service {
  constructor(private items: readonly string[]) {}
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
function format(user: User): string {
  return user.name;
}

class Service {
  constructor(private items: string[]) {}
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
'zero-tolerance/prefer-readonly-parameters': 'error'

'zero-tolerance/prefer-readonly-parameters': [
  'error',
  {
    ignoredTypeNamePatterns: ['^Dispatch$', '(Callback|Handler)$'],
  },
]
Option Type Default Description ignoredTypeNamePatterns string[] ['^Dispatch$', '^Function$', '^RefCallback$', '^VoidFunction$', '(Callback\|Handler)$'] Type-reference names excluded from readonly wrapping

docs.title: Autofix Notes
docs.text:
Autofix can safely:

  • wrap mutable type references as Readonly<T>
  • rewrite mutable array and tuple annotations to readonly ...
  • apply those rewrites to constructor parameter properties as well

Autofix skips type references whose terminal name matches ignoredTypeNamePatterns. This prevents callable aliases such as React Dispatch<SetStateAction<T>> from being rewritten to Readonly<Dispatch<SetStateAction<T>>>, which would remove the callable contract.

Autofix intentionally skips structural rewrites such as mutable inline object type literals.

docs.title: prefer-result-return
docs.text: Prefer returning Result-style values instead of throwing.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended off Strict warn

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Returning typed error values keeps failures explicit in function signatures and avoids hidden control-flow jumps from thrown exceptions.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
function parse(input: string) {
  return { ok: false as const, error: 'invalid' };
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
function parse(input: string) {
  throw new Error('invalid');
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/prefer-result-return': 'warn'

docs.title: prefer-shortcut-return
docs.text: Prefer shortcut boolean returns over if branches that return true/false.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (code) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: When code branches only to return opposite boolean literals, the extra control flow is unnecessary. A direct return is shorter and easier to read.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
function isReady(value: unknown): boolean {
  return !!value;
}

function isDisabled(value: unknown): boolean {
  return !value;
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
function isReady(value: unknown): boolean {
  if (value) return true;
  return false;
}

function isDisabled(value: unknown): boolean {
  if (value) {
    return false;
  } else {
    return true;
  }
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/prefer-shortcut-return': 'error'

docs.title: Behavioral contract
docs.text: The rule skips a replacement when its full source span contains comments, including comments between the if and the following return. This retains explanations and tool directives. Eligible rewrites use !! or ! so falsy parameters still return booleans.

docs.title: prefer-string-raw
docs.text:
Prefer String.raw for string literals that contain escaped backslashes.

This mirrors Sonar rule typescript:S7780.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (--fix) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Strings containing escaped backslashes are harder to read and easier to get wrong. Using String.raw avoids double escaping and keeps path-like and regex-source text easier to maintain.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
const path = String.raw`C:\Users\dev\repo`;
const regexSource = String.raw`\d+\w+`;

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
const path = 'C:\\Users\\dev\\repo';
const regexSource = '\\d+\\w+';

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/prefer-string-raw': 'error'

docs.title: Autofix Notes
docs.text:
Autofix rewrites only eligible string literals to String.raw\`` form after verifying that the resulting template has the same runtime value. Regex literals are never considered; regex-source strings with redundant backslash escaping are fixed only when their value is preserved.

The rule intentionally skips grammar-sensitive positions such as directives, import/export sources, non-computed property keys, JSX attributes, inline Jest snapshots, and TypeScript literal contexts. It also skips mixed runtime escapes, trailing backslashes, multiline strings, template interpolation markers such as ${...}, and backticks.

docs.title: Behavioral contract
docs.text:
Autofix also skips any lexical scope that declares String, including function parameters and bindings declared later in the block. This prevents a new reference from calling a local replacement or entering its temporal dead zone. Scope checks are performed separately for every literal; leaving a shadowed function restores normal handling. The rule assumes the global built-in has not been monkey-patched.

An explicitly disabled String global also prevents a fix, even when TypeScript still exposes its built-in symbol in the scope.

docs.title: prefer-structured-clone
docs.text: Report JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value)) for manual review.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended off Strict off

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: JSON cloning and structuredClone have different value semantics. JSON cloning drops undefined object properties and serializes dates as strings; structured cloning retains undefined properties and Date values. JSON serialization can also invoke toJSON. The rule is opt-in and does not autofix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value)) is reported when the rule is enabled. structuredClone(value) and ordinary JSON.parse(serializedValue) are allowed. Review the data shape and required output before replacing the cloning operation.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: 'zero-tolerance/prefer-structured-clone': 'warn'

docs.title: require-barrel-relative-exports
docs.text: Require barrel re-export declarations to use current-directory descendant paths.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (code) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Barrel files (index.*) should aggregate modules that live under the same directory tree. Re-export paths such as ../foo, @/foo, package-name, or /root/foo make the barrel depend on code outside its local subtree and blur what that barrel actually owns.

This rule applies only to re-export declarations inside barrel files, including:

  • export { foo } from '...'
  • export type { Foo } from '...'
  • export * from '...'
  • export * as ns from '...'

Allowed barrel re-export paths must start with ./ and point at a descendant module such as ./foo or ./feature/foo.

docs.title: Autofix
docs.text: Bare same-directory exports such as export { foo } from 'foo' are fixed to ./foo only when the sibling file or directory can be verified from the linted filename. Package, alias, absolute, parent, virtual, and unverified paths remain report-only.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
// index.ts
export { parseUser } from './parse-user';
export * from './feature/utils';
export type { User } from './types/user';
export * as formatters from './formatters';

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
// index.ts
export { parseUser } from '../parse-user';
export type { User } from '@/types/user';
export * from 'shared/utils';
export * as rootValue from '/root/value';

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/require-barrel-relative-exports': 'error'

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The rule applies only to single-extension barrel files such as index.ts, index.js, and index.mts.
  • Double-extension files such as index.d.ts, index.test.ts, and index.spec.js are ignored.
  • Local export declarations with no from source are not checked by this rule; require-clean-barrel handles those barrel-shape constraints.

docs.title: require-bdd-spec
docs.text: Enforce that every TypeScript source file has a valid sibling .ts.bdd.json BDD specification file.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended off Strict off

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Every non-test TypeScript source file in the plugin must be accompanied by a sibling .ts.bdd.json file that documents its behaviour in BDD (Given/When/Then) format. The rule verifies the repository relationships available while ESLint is parsing the source: sibling presence, the exact sourceFile reference, and parity between module.exports and named exports discovered from the Program AST.

BDD document structure is intentionally validated only once, by pnpm validate:bdd. That command compiles the canonical bdd-spec.schema.json with Ajv, so required fields, types, scenario collections, and scenario naming have one implementation and one source of truth.

This rule is intentionally opt-in and is disabled by default in the built-in recommended and strict presets. Enable it explicitly for repositories that require BDD spec files.

{
  "$schema": "../../../../bdd-spec.schema.json",

  "sourceFile": "packages/plugin/src/rules/my-rule.ts",

          "then": "a violation is reported with the correct message"

    }

}

docs.title: require-clean-barrel
docs.text: Require barrel files (index.*) to contain only module re-export declarations.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Barrel files should stay focused on aggregation. Allowing imports, declarations, executable statements, or local exports inside index.* files mixes concerns and makes module boundaries harder to reason about.

When an index.* file contains at least one module re-export declaration, this rule treats it as a barrel and enforces module re-exports only, such as:

  • export { foo } from './foo'
  • export * from './foo'
  • export type { Foo } from './types'

This rule validates barrel shape only. Re-export source paths inside barrels are governed separately by require-barrel-relative-exports.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
export { createClient } from './create-client';
export { parseConfig } from './parse-config';
export type { ClientOptions } from './types';

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
import { createClient } from './create-client';

export const version = '1.0.0';

const helper = () => {};
export { helper };

This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/require-clean-barrel': 'error'

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The rule applies only to single-extension barrel files such as index.ts, index.js, and index.mts.
  • Double-extension files such as index.d.ts, index.test.ts, and index.spec.js are ignored.

docs.title: require-error-cause
docs.text:
Keep the original exception when throwing a replacement error.

Type: problem. No automatic fix. Enable this rule individually; it is not included in a preset.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Checks replacement errors thrown directly inside a catch block. Supports Error, TypeError, RangeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError, URIError, EvalError, and AggregateError, with or without new.

The cause must refer to the exception caught by that block. Stable aliases and TypeScript assertions preserve that identity. A different value with a matching type does not.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
try {
  readData();
} catch (error) {
  throw new Error('Reading data failed', { cause: error }); // Allowed.
}

try {
  readData();
} catch (error) {
  throw new Error('Reading data failed'); // Reported: loses the original exception.
}

Rethrowing the original exception is allowed. AggregateError takes its options object as the third argument. Nested catch blocks must preserve their own caught exception. Use a simple catch parameter when wrapping an error so the original exception remains available.

docs.title: Options
Limits
docs.text:
Reassigning the caught variable before using it as a cause is reported, including conditional writes. An alias or options object that captured the original value before reassignment remains valid. Directly modified options are not trusted. This includes overwriting or deleting a cause through a type assertion or non-null assertion around the options object.

The rule uses source order; it does not trace every possible execution path. Custom or shadowed constructors, nested function bodies, and errors created earlier and thrown through variables are outside its scope.

docs.title: require-exhaustive-switch
docs.text: Require exhaustive switch statements over finite discriminant types.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: When a switch handles a finite set of states, leaving out a case creates a silent branch that will surface later as a bug. Exhaustive switching keeps state changes visible when unions, booleans, or enums evolve.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
type Status = 'idle' | 'loading';

function render(status: Status): number {
  switch (status) {
    case 'idle':
      return 0;
    case 'loading':
      return 1;
  }
}

function render(flag: boolean): number {
  switch (flag) {
    case true:
      return 1;
    case false:
      return 0;
  }
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
type Status = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success';

function render(status: Status): number {
  switch (status) {
    case 'idle':
      return 0;
    case 'loading':
      return 1;
  }
  return 2;
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

'zero-tolerance/require-exhaustive-switch': 'error'

docs.title: Type Information
docs.text: This rule relies on typed linting so it can enumerate finite union, enum, and boolean cases from the TypeScript checker.

docs.title: require-exported-object-type
docs.text: Require exported object constants to declare an explicit type annotation.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Exported object constants become part of a module's public contract. Requiring an explicit annotation prevents large inferred structural types from leaking through exports and keeps the intended shape readable even when the value is wrapped in Object.freeze(...).

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
export const StatusMap: Readonly<Record<string, string>> = Object.freeze({
  Active: 'active',
  Inactive: 'inactive',
});

type StatusLookup = Record<string, string>;

const StatusMap: StatusLookup = {
  Active: 'active',
};

export { StatusMap };

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
export const StatusMap = Object.freeze({
  Active: 'active',
  Inactive: 'inactive',
});

const StatusMap = {
  Active: 'active',
};

export { StatusMap };

The rule only applies when the exported const initializer is an object literal or Object.freeze({ ... }). Calls such as Object.freeze() or Object.freeze(...values) are ignored because they do not expose a direct frozen object literal shape.

docs.title: require-interface-prefix
docs.text: Enforce that TypeScript interface names start with I (capital letter) followed by an uppercase character.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (code) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Prefixing interface names with I makes it immediately clear in code that a type is an interface rather than a class or type alias. This convention improves readability, especially in large codebases where interfaces are heavily used.

docs.title: Autofix
docs.text: The fixer prefixes capitalized interface names and same-file type references when the generated name does not collide with an existing top-level interface or type alias. Multiple invalid interfaces normally rename in one combined pass. Later reports also offer their own fixes, so suppressing the first report does not remove fixes for other interfaces. Merged declarations sharing a name are updated exactly once per identifier. Lowercase names and collision cases remain report-only.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
interface IUser {
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

interface IRepository<T> {
  findById(id: string): Promise<T>;
}

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
interface User {
  name: string;
}

interface userProfile {
  age: number;
}

docs.text:
This rule has no options. Enable it in your ESLint config:

'zero-tolerance/require-interface-prefix': 'error'

docs.title: require-jsdoc-anonymous-functions
docs.text: Require JSDoc documentation comments on anonymous function-like constructs outside of test files, such as anonymous default exports, computed methods without identifier keys, and inline anonymous callbacks. Anonymous callbacks passed to well-known test APIs such as describe, it, test, beforeEach, and afterAll are excluded.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (--fix) Recommended off Strict off

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Anonymous functions hide intent at the callsite and can make behavior harder to understand in larger codebases. Requiring JSDoc on anonymous function-like constructs makes their purpose explicit and improves generated documentation quality.

This rule is automatically skipped in test files (.test.* / .spec.*). It also skips anonymous callbacks passed to common test framework APIs and hook helpers, including chained forms such as describe.only(...), test.skip.each(...), and test.beforeEach(...).

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
/**
 * Creates the default app configuration.
 */
export default function () {
  return { retries: 3 };
}

class Registry {
  /**
   * Handles computed command dispatch.
   */
  ['run']() {}
}

describe('CLI knowledge-base command', () => {
  it('should register the command', () => {
    expect(getKnowledgeBaseCommand()).toBeDefined();
  });
});

docs.title: ❌ Incorrect
docs.text:
export default function () {
  return { retries: 3 };
}

class Registry {
  ['run']() {}
}

registerCommand(() => {
  return buildCommand();
});

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This rule has no options:

// Opt in when anonymous function JSDoc is required for your codebase.
'zero-tolerance/require-jsdoc-anonymous-functions': 'warn'

docs.title: Autofix Notes
docs.text:
Autofix can insert a missing JSDoc block for standalone anonymous targets such as default export functions.

Autofix intentionally skips unsafe insertion targets such as inline expressions and multi-declarator variable statements.

docs.title: Test files and test callbacks are exempt
docs.text:
Functions inside files matching *.test.ts, *.spec.ts, *.test.js, *.spec.js (and their JSX equivalents) are not checked.

Anonymous callbacks passed to well-known test APIs such as describe, it, test, beforeAll, beforeEach, afterAll, and afterEach are also not checked, even when they appear in non-test files.

docs.title: require-jsdoc-functions
docs.text: Require JSDoc documentation comments on named function-like constructs outside of test files, including declarations, named variable-assigned function expressions, named arrow functions, class methods, static methods, class field functions, and object methods.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (--fix) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
JSDoc comments are essential for self-documenting code and support IDE tooling, generated API documentation, and clear intent communication to future maintainers. Every @param tag must include both the parameter name and a non-empty functional description; a bare tag such as @param tools does not satisfy the rule. This rule is automatically skipped in test files (.test.* / .spec.*).

Anonymous function-like constructs are enforced by the companion rule require-jsdoc-anonymous-functions.

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text:
/**
 * Fetches a user record by ID.
 * @param id - User identifier to retrieve.

 */

/**

/**
 * Returns a normalized display label.

 */

class DedupeFactory {

docs.title: require-node-protocol
docs.text: Require Node.js built-in module imports to use the node: protocol prefix.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable Yes (code) Recommended warn Strict error

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Starting with Node.js 16, built-in modules can be imported using the node: protocol prefix (e.g., node:fs instead of fs). Using the protocol prefix makes it immediately clear that the import refers to a Node.js built-in module rather than a user-land package with the same name, improving readability and preventing potential name collisions.

import path from 'node:path';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import os from 'node:os';
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

docs.title: require-optional-chaining
docs.text: Report repeated && guard access for manual review.

docs.title: Rule Details
docs.text: Property Value Type suggestion Fixable No Recommended off Strict off

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: value && value.member and value?.member can return different values when value is falsy but not nullish. For example, text && text.length returns an empty string for text = '', while text?.length returns zero. Repeated member access can also invoke getters twice. The rule is opt-in and does not autofix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: user && user.profile is reported when the rule is enabled. user?.profile and unrelated logical guards are allowed. Check falsy values and getter behavior before changing a reported expression.

docs.title: Rationale

type Props = { name: string };
